items.text: Not locked into starting role. Caruso will compete in training camp for the starting point guard job with the Bulls, K.C. Johnson of NBC Sports Chicago reports. The 29-year-old was named to the NBA All-Defensive First Team last season, but that accolade won't guarantee Caruso a starting gig. Health could be the Bulls' biggest concern with him, as Caruso has missed 56 of a possible 164 games over the last two seasons with Chicago due to various injuries, and the franchise is already dealing with one injured point guard in Lonzo Ball, who will miss the entire 2023-24 campaign due to knee issues. Caruso will compete with Coby White, Jevon Carter and Ayo Dosunmu for the starting job.

Keep availability in mind. Horford will likely rest during back-to-backs and "can at the very least be expected to miss 14 games," writes Jay King of The Athletic. Horford sitting at least one game of back-to-backs is logical as he enters his age-37 campaign, and it's a continuation of Horford's resting pattern down the stretch last year. Excluding his brief Oklahoma City tenure, Horford has appeared in at least 67 games in every campaign since 2013, but that is likely to change.

Sustains right ankle sprain. Pokusevski (arm) sustained a right ankle sprain during an offseason workout Tuesday and will be re-evaluated in six weeks, Brandon Rahbar of DailyThunder.com reports. Pokusevski suffered a small right humerus fracture at the beginning of June and was unable to play for the Serbian national team in the FIBA World Cup as a result. Although he was evidently cleared to resume working out, he's now dealing with an ankle issue that will force him to miss several weeks and could sideline him for the start of the regular season. Pokusevski has had a relatively consistent role over his first three seasons with the Thunder, averaging 8.0 points, 4.9 rebounds and 2.1 assists in 21.7 minutes per game.

Won't play in World Cup. Pokusevski won't play for Serbia in the 2023 FIBA World Cup, Eurohoops.net reports. The 17th overall pick of the 2020 NBA Draft, Pokusevski suffered a broken arm during an offseason workout at the end of May and won't receive medical clearance to train with a basketball until late August, meaning he won't be able to recover in time to play in the tournament. The 21-year-old was hoping to secure a spot on the Serbian national team's 12-man roster, but the injury will prevent him from doing so.

Dominates glass. Sengun posted 16 points (6-16 FG, 4-6 FT), 12 rebounds, four blocks and three assists in 26 minutes during Friday's 110-104 preseason win over the Heat. Sengun recorded a game-high seven offensive rebounds in Friday's victory. Against Miami, the third-year center had his best preseason outing. Sengun is expected to start alongside Jabari Smith in Houston's frontcourt this season.

Getting veteran guidance. Sengun has been consulting Jeff Green on preparation practices of Nikola Jokic, Kelly Iko of The Athletic reports. Comparisons between Sengun and Jokic are premature at this stage, but the 21-year-old is among the top passing bigs in the league. Sengun averaged 18.4 points, 11.2 rebounds and 4.8 assists per 36 minutes last season, joining Jokic, Domantas Sabonis and Giannis Antetokounmpo as the only players to do so. Green, who spent the past two seasons with Denver, added that Sengun "sees the comparisons [to Jokic] but he's trying to better himself...he sees Joker as a standard, but [Sengun] wants to be better."

However, the injury shouldn't be overly serious, and the highly-touted prospect should be fully healthy by the start of training camp in September. Might play for Team USA in 2024. Davis is among the star players that LeBron James has reached out to ahead of the 2024 Olympics, Shams Charania of The Athletic reports. James has set his sights on playing for Team USA during the upcoming 2024 Olympics, but he is also targeting several top players to join him in a star-studded roster, and Davis is among the players whom the Lakers star is targeting as potential teammates. The star big man has won gold medals in both the 2012 Olympics and the 2014 World Cup, making him the first player in basketball history to win an NCAA title, NBA title, Olympic gold medal and FIBA World Cup.

The 22-year-old continues to serve as the backcourt focal point of an otherwise frontcourt-heavy roster.

The 22-year-old was a force on both ends as well, routinely picking up tough assignments while accumulating 1.6 steals-plus-blocks per game. Edwards is blossoming into a player with MVP-caliber upside.

Awarded for stellar play. Bogdanovic was named to the World Cup All-Star 5 on Sunday, via FIBA's official release. Bogdanovic averaged 19.1 points, 3.3 rebounds, 4.6 assists and 2.1 steals in 27.8 minutes per game during Serbia's run to the FIBA World Cup Championship. Serbia was defeated 83-77 by Germany on Sunday. Bogdanovic was one of three tournament qualifiers to average 19-plus points and two-plus steals per game. The 31-year-old being healthy and carrying momentum into the 2023-24 season bodes well for his outlook, as he should play a critical scoring role in coach Quin Snyder's offense.

Reaves played a team-high 23 minutes Thursday and tied LeBron James for the most three-pointers made with three. While the third-year guard posted impressive defensive numbers, he was the only Lakers starter to record a negative point differential (-3). Reaves is set to be Los Angeles' starting shooting guard for the 2023-24 campaign.

Even though Team USA won't earn the gold medal following their semifinal loss against Germany, the program may have developed some intriguing players for the 2024 Olympics and beyond. Reaves could be one of those players, as he averaged 12.4 points and 1.3 steals per game before the third-place matchup against Canada, both being top-3 marks among the team, and he has been on the court in close games as well. The Lakers guard has several traits that adjust quite well to the international stage.

Headed to Phoenix. Bol agreed to a one-year deal with the Suns on Sunday, Adrian Wojnarowski of ESPN reports. Bol was surprisingly waived by the Magic in early July, and his name was immediately mentioned as a target for the star-laden Suns. The 2019 second-round pick flashed his potential in 2022-23, averaging 9.1 points, 5.8 rebounds, 1.2 blocks and 1.0 assists in 21.5 minutes per game while starting 33 of his 70 appearances -- all career highs. Given Phoenix's top-heavy rotation, Bol has a chance to carve out a solid reserve role behind Kevin Durant and Deandre Ayton (ribs) during the 2023-24 campaign.

May be headed to Phoenix. The Suns are viewed as the top contenders in the race to sign Bol, Shams Charania of The Athletic reports. Bol hit waivers Tuesday after the Magic decided to part ways with him before his 2023-24 salary became guaranteed, and as a result, he's now free to join any team as a free agent. Rival teams are expecting Bol to sign with Phoenix on a veteran-minimum deal, but it's worth noting the promising big man is coming off the best season of his career. He averaged 9.1 points, 5.8 rebounds and 1.2 blocks in 21.5 minutes per game across 70 appearances during the 2022-23 campaign.

Leads team in scoring Tuesday. Ingram delivered 18 points (8-16 FG, 0-1 3Pt, 2-2 FT), four rebounds and six assists across 24 minutes in Tuesday's 104-92 preseason win over the Magic. Ingram is ramping up following a busy summer in which he represented Team USA in the 2023 FIBA World Cup, and all signs point to him being ready to open the season as one of the Pelicans' go-to players on both ends of the court. Ingram is aiming to top what he did last season when he averaged 24.7 points, 5.8 assists and 5.5 rebounds per game while operating as the Pelicans' go-to player on offense, though it's worth noting he featured in only 45 games and most of that production came with Zion Williamson sidelined.

No extension until next summer. Ingram indicated Monday he has no interest in signing an extension with the Pelicans until after this season is over, Christian Clark of The New Orleans Times-Picayune reports. "They handing a lot of people big money. I'm trying to get some big money," Ingram said. The 26-year-old forward is already eligible for a contract extension, but any deal he signed now would be capped in value at about $160 million for three years. By waiting until next summer, Ingram would instead be eligible for an extension worth up to about $220 for four years, and should he get named to an All-NBA Team in 2023-34, that would skyrocket to a super-max contract worth over $330 million for five seasons. The Pelicans may not be willing to pay him the absolute maximum, of course, but as long as he stays healthy this season, Ingram has little to lose and an awful lot to gain by delaying extension talks.
